title: Pauri 33, sound: aakhan jor
tomorrow: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own

cards: Ever tried not to laugh? A quiet classroom, a serious meeting, a moment when laughing is the worst thing you could do. And it rises anyway.
You bite your cheek, you stare at the floor, and your shoulders shake. Or the opposite: you want to say the right thing to a grieving friend, and nothing comes out at all.
Speaking and staying quiet look like the two things a person controls best. Pauri 33 opens with exactly those two, and one hard little word that keeps coming back like a hammer.

teach.b: The first line: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Four sounds. Aakhan: speaking, saying; it echoes aakheeah from yesterday, where the Name was said on a million tongues.
Jor: power, force, strength, still alive in everyday Punjabi when people mean push hard, put your strength into it.

teach.h: CHUPAI NAH JOR — NOR TO BE SILENT.
teach.b: Chupai: in silence; you may know chup from Punjabi, as in chup kar, be quiet. Nah: not, no. So: no power to speak, no power to keep silent.
Commentators read that nah across both halves. Now the shape. Jor lands at the end of each half: two short beats, then the heavy one.
The next line flips it, so jor comes first and last: jor na mangan, den na jor. No power to ask, no power to give. The word boxes the line in.

teach.h: JOR, AGAIN AND AGAIN, LIKE A HAMMER.
teach.b: The whole stanza keeps doing this: jor ten times in eight short lines, nine of them with na or nah beside it, like knocking on door after door and finding each one locked.
Tomorrow, which doors, and whose hand holds the key. Today, feel the hammer. You can almost recite this stanza by its rhythm alone.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33's repeated word jor, power, gives it a strong, hammering rhythm.

games.q: the sound of Pauri 33 — tap the pairs.

s: the second line has jor first and last
jor na mangan, den na jor: no power to ask, no power to give.
jor appears only once in Pauri 33
it comes back ten times in eight short lines, like a hammer.
the first line is about power to speak and to be silent

games.q: Pauri 33 opens with speaking and silence. what does the first line say about them?
o: we have full power over both.
there's no power in us to speak, nor to keep silent.
games.why: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. tomorrow: whose hand holds the power instead.

practice: Say the first line aloud three times, slowly, letting jor land heavy like a hand on a table: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor; then the next one, jor na mangan, den na jor. Then stop speaking and simply stay silent.
Even the silence isn't quite yours, since thoughts keep talking; don't fight them, let them knock and pass.

wordCard.voice: Chupai, silence. It opens: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor, no power to speak, no power to be silent, and the word jor keeps coming back like a hammer.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 33: no power to speak, no power to keep silent.

carryVoice: Your line: aakhan jor. Even speech and silence aren't fully in our power. Until tomorrow.
